topic.name: Tangent Vectors and Tangent Lines to Curves

question.text: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $\mathbf r(t)=\left\langle t, \: e^t, \:e^{-t}\right\rangle$ at the point where $t=0,$ valid for all real values of $u?$
question.explanation:
At the point where $t=0$, the vector $\mathbf r'\left(0\right )$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

\[ \mathbf R(u)=\mathbf r\left(0\right )+u\mathbf r'\left(0\right ), \quad u \in (-\infty, \infty) \]

First, we find $\mathbf r\left(0\right )\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \mathbf r(0 ) &= \left\langle 0, \: e^0, \:e^{-0}\right\rangle \\[3pt] &= \left\langle 0, \: 1, \: 1\right\rangle \end{align*}

Now, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) &=\left\langle \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(t), \: \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(e^t), \:\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(e^{-t})\right\rangle \\[3pt] &=\left\langle 1, \: e^t, \:-e^{-t}\right\rangle \end{align*}

Then, we evaluate $\mathbf r'(t)$ at $t=0\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \mathbf r'(0) &=\left\langle 1, \: e^0, \:-e^{-0}\right\rangle\\[3pt] &=\left\langle 1, \: 1, \:-1\right\rangle \end{align*}

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where $t=0$ is
\[ \mathbf R(u)=\left\langle 0, \: 1, \: 1\right\rangle +u\left\langle 1, \: 1, \:-1\right\rangle, \quad u \in (-\infty, \infty). \]

example.title: Finding a Tangent Line to a Curve

question.text: Given the curve $\mathbf r(t) = \left\langle -\dfrac{2t^3}{3} , 2t - 1\right\rangle,$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $\left\langle -1, -1 \right\rangle.$
question.explanation:
First, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf r(t)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) & = \left\langle \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left( -\dfrac{2t^3}{3}\right) , \, \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\left( 2t - 1\right)\right\rangle\\[5pt] & = \left\langle -2t^2 , 2 \right\rangle \end{align*}

The vectors $\left\langle -1, -1\right\rangle$ and $\mathbf r'(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $\left\langle -1 , -1\right\rangle \cdot \mathbf r'(t) = 0.$ So, we have \begin{align*} \left\langle -1 , -1\right\rangle \cdot \mathbf r'(t) & = 0 \\[5pt] \left\langle -1 , -1 \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle -2t^2 , 2 \right\rangle & = 0 \\[5pt] (-1)(-2t^2) + (-1)(2) & = 0\\[5pt] 2t^2 - 2 & = 0\\[5pt] 2(t+1)(t-1) & = 0. \end{align*}

Therefore, the solutions are $t = \pm{1}.$

Finally, since \begin{align*} \mathbf r(-1) & = \left\langle -\dfrac{2(-1)^3}{3} , 2(-1) - 1\right\rangle = \left\langle \dfrac{2}{3} , -3 \right\rangle, \\[5pt] \mathbf r(1) & = \left\langle -\dfrac{2(1)^3}{3} , 2(1) - 1\right\rangle = \left\langle -\dfrac{2}{3} , 1 \right\rangle, \end{align*} we conclude that $\left\langle -1 , -1\right\rangle$ and $\mathbf r'(t)$ are perpendicular at the points $\left(-\dfrac{2}{3},1\right)$ and $\left(\dfrac{2}{3},-3\right).$

example.title: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Perpendicular to Another Vector

question.text: Given the curve $\mathbf r(t)=\left\langle t^2+1\,,\, 2t-1\right\rangle,$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $\left\langle 1\,,\, -2\right\rangle.$
question.explanation:
First, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf r(t)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) &=\left\langle \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}\big(t^2 +1\big)\,,\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t} (2t-1)\right\rangle\\[5pt] &=\left\langle 2t \,,\, 2\right\rangle \end{align*}

The vectors $\left\langle 1\,,\, -2 \right\rangle$ and $\mathbf r'(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $\left\langle 1\,,\, -2 \right\rangle \cdot \mathbf r'(t) = 0.$ So, we have

\begin{align*} \left\langle 1\,,\, -2\right\rangle \cdot \mathbf r'(t) &= 0 \\[3pt] \left\langle 1\,,\, -2\right\rangle \cdot \left\langle 2t \,,\, 2 \right\rangle &= 0 \\[3pt] 1 \cdot 2t + (-2) \cdot 2 &= 0 \\[3pt] 2t - 4 &= 0 \\[3pt] 2(t-2) &= 0. \end{align*}

Therefore, the only solution is $t=2.$

Finally, since

\begin{align*} \mathbf r(2) &= \left\langle \left(2\right)^2+1\,,\, 2\left(2\right)-1 \right\rangle = \left\langle 5\,,\, 3 \right\rangle, \end{align*}

we conclude that $\left\langle 1\,,\, -2\right\rangle$ and $\mathbf r'(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $\left(5,3\right).$

example.title: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Perpendicular to Another Vector

question.text: Given the curve $\mathbf r(t)=\left\langle t^4+4t\,,\, t^3-2t \,,\, 2t^3-3t\right\rangle,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $\left\langle 0\,,\, 1 \,,\, 3\right\rangle.$
question.explanation:
First, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf r(t)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) &=\left\langle \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(t^4+4t), \: \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(t^3-2t), \: \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(2t^3 - 3t) \right\rangle \\[5pt] &=\left\langle 4t^3 +4, \: 3t^2 - 2, \: 6t^2-3 \right\rangle \end{align*}

The vectors $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $\left\langle 0\,,\, 1 \,,\, 3\right\rangle$ are parallel for some specific value $t_0$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $\mathbf r'(t_0) = c \,\left\langle 0\,,\, 1 \,,\, 3\right\rangle.$ So, we have

\begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) &= c \,\left\langle 0\,,\, 1 \,,\, 3\right\rangle \\[3pt] \left\langle 4t^3 +4, \: 3t^2 -2, \: 6t^2-3 \right\rangle &=c \, \left\langle 0\,,\, 1 \,,\, 3\right\rangle \\[3pt] \left\langle 4t^3 +4, \: 3t^2 -2, \: 6t^2-3 \right\rangle &= \left\langle 0\,,\, c \,,\, 3c \right\rangle. \end{align*}

Equating the components gives:

\[ \begin{cases} 4t^3 + 4 = 0 \\ 3t^2-2 = c \\ 6t^2 - 3 = 3c \end{cases} \]

From the first equation, we obtain that $t=-1.$ Substituting to the second equation, we get $c=1.$ These values also satisfy the third equation.

Therefore, $\left\langle 0\,,\, 1 \,,\, 3\right\rangle$ and $\mathbf r'$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=-1.$

Finally, since \begin{align*} \mathbf r(-1) &= \left\langle (-1)^4+4(-1)\,,\, (-1)^3-2(-1) \,,\, 2(-1)^3-3(-1)\right\rangle \\[3pt] &= \left\langle -3, \: 1, \: 1\right\rangle, \end{align*}

we conclude that $\left\langle 0\,,\, 1 \,,\, 3\right\rangle$ and $\mathbf r'(t)$ are parallel at the point $(-3, 1 , 1).$

example.title: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Parallel to Another Vector

question.text: Given the curve $\mathbf r(t)=\left\langle \sqrt{t}\,,\, t^3+5 \,,\, 2t+2 \right\rangle,$ $t \in (0,\infty),$ find all of the points at which $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $\mathbf r(t)$ are parallel.
question.explanation:
First, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf r(t)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \mathbf r'(t) &=\left\langle \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(\sqrt{t}), \: \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(t^3+5), \: \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}t}(2t+2) \right\rangle \\[5pt] &=\left\langle \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}, \: 3t^2, \: 2 \right\rangle \end{align*}

The vectors $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $\mathbf r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value $t_0$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $\mathbf r(t_0) = c \, \mathbf r'(t_0).$ So, we have

\begin{align*} \mathbf r(t) &= c \, \mathbf r'(t) \\[3pt] \left\langle \sqrt{t}, \: t^3+5, \: 2t+2\right\rangle &=c \, \left\langle \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}, \: 3t^2, \: 2\right\rangle \\[3pt] \left\langle \sqrt{t}, \: t^3+5, \:2t+2\right\rangle &=\left\langle \dfrac{c}{2\sqrt{t}}, \: 3ct^2, \: 2c\right\rangle. \end{align*}

Equating the components gives:

\[ \begin{cases} \sqrt{t}= \dfrac{c}{2\sqrt{t}} \\[3pt] t^3+5 = 3ct^2 \\[3pt] 2t+2 = 2c \end{cases} \]

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=2t.$ Substituting into the third equation, we get

\begin{align*} 2t +2 &= 2\cdot (2t) \\ 2t+2 &= 4t \\ 2t -2 &= 0 \\ t &= 1. \end{align*}

This satisfies also the second equation $t^3+5 = 3ct^2.$

Therefore, $\mathbf r$ and $\mathbf r'$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=1.$ These values also satisfy the second equation.

Finally, since \begin{align*} \mathbf r(1) &= \left\langle \sqrt{1}\,,\, 1^3+5 \,,\, 2(1)+2 \right\rangle \\[3pt] &= \left\langle 1, \: 6, \: 4\right\rangle, \end{align*}

we conclude that $\mathbf r(t)$ and $\mathbf r'(t)$ are parallel at the point $(1,6,4).$
